latin_text: PRISCÆ illius ignorantiæ^a temporibus, quæ salutarem Christi adventum præcesserunt, Britannos et Hibernos nostros communem reliquarum gentium sortem subiisse, id est, “fuisse^b absque Christo, alienos a republica Israelis, et extraneos quod ad fœdera promissionis attinet, spem non habentes, et sine Deo in mundo:” non est quod quisquam dubitet. “Neque enim Britannia fertilis provincia tyrannorum,” inquiebat olim impius Porphyrius^c, “et Scoticæ gentes omnesque usque ad oceanum per circuitum barbaræ nationes Moysen prophetasque cognoverant.” Neque minus falluntur viri^d docti, qui Britannos a Druydibus suis in unius Dei cultu semper institutos fuisse tradunt, quam nugatus est Postellus, quum ab Hebræis^e Hibernorum originem conatus est arcessere. Nam et Origenes^f, quem illi authorem citant, plane contrarium indicat, “terram Britanniæ ante adventum Christi in unius dei religionem” minime consensisse: nominatim vero Andrasten sive Andaten, Victoriæ deam, Dio Cassius^g, Apollinem et Dianam alii a Britannis coli consuevisse prodiderunt: et de eorum idolomania gentilis ipsorum Gildas tam clarum perhibet testimonium, ut res in quæstionem vocari non debeat. Sic enim ille: “Igitur omittens priscos illos communesquc cum omnibus gentibus errores, quibus ante adventum Christi in carne omne humanum genus obligabatur adstrictum; nec enumerans patriæ portenta ipsa diabolica, pene numero Egyptiaca vincentia, quorum nonnulla lineamentis adhuc deformibus intra vel extra deserta mœnia, solito more rigentia torvis vultibus intuemur: neque nominatim inclamitans montes ipsos, aut colles, vel fluvios, olim exitiales, nunc vero humanis usibus utiles, quibus divinus honor a cæco tunc populo cumulabatur, &c.” Ut de illorum temporum miserrima, et subsequentium felicissima conditione, in epitaphio Nepotiani B. Hieronymus pronuntiare non dubitaverit. “Ubi^h tunc totius orbis homines, ab India usque ad Britanniam, a rigida septentrionis plaga usque ad fervores Atlantici oceani tam innumerabiles populi, et tantarum gentium multitudines; Quam^i variæ linguis, habitu tam vestis et armis?

translation_history.english: No one need doubt that, in those times of ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish underwent the common lot of the other nations — that is, that they were “without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers as regards the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” For, as the impious Porphyry once said, “neither had Britain, a province fertile in tyrants, nor the Scottish peoples and all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, known Moses and the prophets.” Nor are the learned men who maintain that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of one God any less mistaken than Postel was when he trifled in attempting to derive the origin of the Irish from the Hebrews. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, indicates plainly the contrary — that “the land of Britain, before the advent of Christ, by no means agreed in the religion of one God”; and specifically Dio Cassius has recorded that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons; and concerning their idol-madness their own countryman Gildas furnishes so clear a testimony that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: “Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, common to all the nations, by which the whole human race was bound fast before the advent of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of my country, almost exceeding in number those of Egypt, some of which we still behold, with their features yet misshapen, within or without the deserted walls, rigid after the usual manner with their grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once deadly but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, &c.” So that the blessed Jerome, in his epitaph of Nepotian, did not hesitate to pronounce upon the most wretched condition of those times and the most happy condition of those that followed: “Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the rigid region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — peoples so innumerable, and multitudes of nations so great; how varied in their tongues, how varied in the fashion of their dress and their arms?”

translation_history.english: For when the fullness of time had come, “the mystery which had been kept silent from the times of the ages was made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, was declared to all peoples for the obedience of faith.” And from this that light, destined to be revealed to the peoples, shone upon those who were set in darkness and the shadow of death: concerning which God speaks through the prophet, “I have appointed you to be a light to the peoples, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.” For when Christ commanded his apostles to go out into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature, they went out and preached everywhere, so that they allowed no place to remain hidden from the heavenly doctrine; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου [neither the islands, nor the mainland, nor any third dwelling-place that nature had granted to humankind],” as Gregory of Nyssa puts it. And thus was fulfilled what God had once foretold through Isaiah: “I will send some of them to the peoples in the ocean, and to the most remote islands, which had not heard my fame nor seen my glory, that they may declare my glory among the peoples.” For “the word of God,” — these are Augustine’s words — “has been preached not on the continental land alone, but also in the islands, which are set in the midst of the sea: and these too are full of Christians, full of the servants of God. translation_history.english: And indeed, that [Britain] received the Gospel from its very first rising — that to this island stiff with glacial cold and, as though lying in some remoter recess of the lands and not near to the visible sun, that true Sun, shining not from the temporal firmament alone but from the highest citadel of the heavens that surpasses all times, displaying to the whole world the radiant gleam of himself, first granted his rays in time, as we know, at the close of Tiberius Caesar's reign (when his religion was being propagated without any hindrance — the senate unwilling, but the emperor threatening death against the informers who denounced its adherents) — that is, Christ granted his precepts. And although these were received tepidly by the inhabitants, yet among some entirely and among others less so, they remained until the persecution of Diocletian.” So Gildas; and what he here says about the close of Tiberius's reign must be explained from Eusebius's chronicle, in which, at either the last or the next-to-last year of Tiberius, it is noted: “When Pilate had reported to Tiberius concerning the doctrine of the Christians, Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, that it might be received among the other sacred rites. But when, by the deliberation of the fathers, it had been resolved that the Christians be expelled from the city, Tiberius by edict threatened death to the accusers of the Christians.

translation_history.english: Some report — from the book on the sufferings of the martyrs by Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, written in Arabic — that St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, went away into the west and performed many miracles in those regions. Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that the same man "preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and following him, Freculf of Lisieux. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, likewise asserts that he "preached on the western shores before all the other apostles." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who has put on the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais. For the former says, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41: "On his return James visited Gaul, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest importance." De quibus beatus Hieronymus in suo martyrologio sic dixit, ac beato Chromatio scripsit : quod sepulto in Galæcia beati Jacobi corpore, ab apostolis Petro et Paulo infulis episcopalibus apud Romam ordinantur, et ad prædicandum Dei verbum ad Hispanias, adhuc gentili errore implicatas, diriguntur.

translation_history.english: But others show that James was killed by Herod before the apostles were divided into "the various regions of the world" (as Vincent puts it, following Turpin) — namely, the very authors whom Vincent himself followed. Turpin, in the Life of Charlemagne, and Calixtus II, in the book on the miracles of St. James the apostle and the translation of his body (if indeed one and the same person was not the author of both works), report that these things took place not in Ireland but in Galicia. "The apostle," says Calixtus in his preface, "is said to have chosen nine disciples in Galicia while he was still living: seven of whom, the other two remaining in Galicia to preach, went with him to Jerusalem, and after his passion carried his body by sea to Galicia. Of these the blessed Jerome spoke thus in his martyrology, and wrote to the blessed Chromatius: that, once the body of blessed James had been buried in Galicia, they were ordained at Rome by the apostles Peter and Paul with episcopal mitres, and were sent to preach the word of God to the Spains, still entangled in pagan error."

latin_text: Et ita sane in martyrologio Romano (quod Hieronymi^m nomine olim editum, supposita^n quoque ejusdem ad Chromatium et Heliodorum epistola, confirmat Baronius) ut et in Bedæ, Usuardi, Notkeri et Adonis martyrologiis, ad Idus Maii, legimus; “ Romæ hos a sanctis apostolis episcopos ordinatos, et ad prædicandum verbum Dei in Hispanias directos esse: cumque diversis urbibus evangelizassent, et innumeras multitudines Christi fidei subjugassent ;” tandem in dictis Hispaniæ locis quievisse. In vetere Romanæ Ecclesiæ martyrologio, quod suo præfixit Ado, non aliud de illis dicitur, quam quod “ Romæ ab apostolis^o ordinati sunt.” In Britannico vero^p, quod describendum curavit Ricemarchus Sulgeni Menevensis episcopi filius, ne nominantur quidem. In apostolorum tamen catalogo, qui epistolæ ad Chromatium et Heliodorum ibi subjicitur, de Jacobo legitur: “ Hic Hispaniæ, et in occidentalia loca prædicavit: et sub Herode gladio cæsus occubuit.” Addit Ordericus Vitalis Uticensis monachus, libro secundo ecclesiasticæ historiæ, septem ipsius discipulos cadaver ejus in Hispaniam detulisse, “ et a rege Galliciæ susceptos, primum fidem et religionem Hiberis prædicavisse.” An pro Hiberis Vincentius alicubi Hibernis exaratum repererit, aliis conjiciendum relinquo : certe hujusmodi aliquo errore dictos Jacobi discipulos ad Hiberniam translatos esse, a vero non est absimile.

translation_history.english: And so indeed in the Roman Martyrology (which Baronius confirms was once published under Jerome's name, together with a likewise supposititious letter of the same Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus), as also in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and Ado, at the Ides of May, we read that “these men were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles, and were sent into Spain to preach the word of God; and when they had evangelized in various cities, and had brought countless multitudes under the faith of Christ,” they at last rested in the said places of Spain. In the old martyrology of the Roman Church, which Ado prefixed to his own, nothing else is said of them than that “they were ordained at Rome by the apostles.” But in the British martyrology, which Ricemarchus, son of Sulgenus bishop of Menevia, saw to be transcribed, they are not even named. Yet in the catalogue of the apostles, which is there appended to the letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus, it is recorded of James: “He preached to Spain and to the western regions, and under Herod he fell, slain by the sword.” Orderic Vitalis, the monk of Ouche, adds, in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History, that seven of his disciples carried his body into Spain, “and, being received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians.” Whether Vincent somewhere found “Hiberni” (the Irish) written in place of “Hiberi” (the Iberians), I leave for others to conjecture; certainly it is not far from the truth that, through some error of this kind, the said disciples of James were transferred to Ireland.

latin_text: S. PAULUM doctorem Gentium τὸν^t τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα, (ut de eo loquitur Basilius Seleuciensis) “ ab oceano usque ad oceanum cucurrisse,” affirmat Hieronymus^u: “ imitantem Dominum suum et solem justitiæ, de quo legimus; A^w summo cælo egressio ejus, et occursus ejus, usque ad summum ejus, ut ante eum terra deficeret quam studium prædicandi:” et post primam apologiam, cujus ipse in posteriore ad Timotheum epistola meminit, a Nerone dimissum, evangelium^x Christi in occidentis quoque partibus prædicavisse. Verba apostoli^y sunt : “ In prima mea defensione nemo mihi adfuit; sed omnes me dereliqueruut. Non illis imputetur. Dominus autem mihi adstitit, et confortavit; ut per me prædicatio impleatur, et audiant omnes gentes.” In quem locum Theodoretus: “ Quando,” inquit, “ appellatione usus, Romam a Festo missus est, defensione audita fuit absolutus, et in Hispaniam profectus est, et ad alias gentes excurrens, eis doctrinæ lucem attulit;” atque, ut alibi addit idem^z, “ Insulis quæ in mari jacent, utilitatem attulit.” Unde de eo Venantius Fortunatus^a : Transiit Oceanum, vel qua facit insula portum, Quasque Britannus habet terras, quasque ultima Thule.

translation_history.english: Jerome affirms that St. Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, τὸν τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα [who traversed the inhabited world, and by his race for the faith made the world seem small] (as Basil of Seleucia speaks of him), "ran from ocean to ocean," "imitating his Lord and the sun of righteousness, of whom we read: His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to the highest part of it, so that the earth would sooner fail than his zeal for preaching"; and that, after his first defense — which he himself mentions in the later epistle to Timothy — having been released by Nero, he preached the gospel of Christ in the regions of the West as well. The words of the apostle are: "At my first defense no one stood with me, but all forsook me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and all the Gentiles might hear." On which passage Theodoret says: "When," he says, "having made his appeal, he was sent from Festus to Rome, his defense was heard and he was acquitted, and he set out for Spain, and, running out to other peoples, brought them the light of doctrine"; and, as the same author adds elsewhere, "He brought benefit to the islands that lie in the sea." Whence Venantius Fortunatus says of him: He crossed the Ocean, even where the island makes a harbor, and the lands the Briton holds, and those of farthest Thule.

Et licet sub Trajano mortem poeta obierit: senem tamen decessisse cogitandum est, et prius familiariter usum esse Silio Italico, secundi belli Punici scriptore: quo consulatum gerente, Neronem interiisse, et alii authores confirmant, et ipse Martialis^r significat illis de Silio versiculis : Postquam bis senis ingentem fascibus annum Rexerat, asserto qui sacer orbe fuit : Emeritos Musis et Phœbo tradidit annos, Proque suo celebrat nunc Helicona foro.

translation_history.english: Here the most ingenious critic conjectures that the word "Scotici" should be substituted for "Scythici" — forgetting that in Claudian, Apollinaris Sidonius, and those ancient writers the first syllable of the name "Scoti" is always read long, and that in old manuscripts "Scotti" was regularly written throughout with a doubled letter. And he is quite in character when he adds that Persons "proves, in his "Conversion of England," that Claudia could not have been an Englishwoman" — as though anyone would rave with Dempster's madness and search for England in Britain in Claudia's day, or as though Persons were not trying to establish by his argument that the blessed Claudia whom Paul mentions was not that British woman whose beauty Martial praised under the emperor Trajan, and was consequently set up, without any foundation, as either a Scotswoman or an Englishwoman. And yet that argument on which he chiefly relies, drawn from chronological reckoning, carries little weight. For even if, in the eleventh book of epigrams which I cited, there occur certain poems composed under the third consulship of either Nerva or Trajan, it does not follow that all the rest were composed at the same time. And although the poet died under Trajan, it must be supposed that he died an old man, and that he had earlier been on familiar terms with Silius Italicus, the writer on the Second Punic War — during whose consulship Nero perished, as both other authorities confirm and Martial himself indicates in those verses about Silius: "After he had governed the mighty year with its twice-six fasces — he who was hallowed when the world had been set free — he gave his retirement years to the Muses and to Phoebus, and now frequents Helicon in place of his own forum."

latin_text: Nerone vero summam rerum obtinente (et quidem, ut pluribus placet, sub finem imperii illius) a Paulo illa scripta est epistola, in qua Timotheum salutant Pudens et Linus et Claudia. Sed de his in capite tertio iterum etiam erit dicendi locus.

translation_history.english: While Nero held the supreme power (and indeed, as most hold, toward the end of his reign), Paul wrote that epistle in which Pudens, Linus, and Claudia greet Timothy. But there will be occasion to speak of these again in chapter three.
